title: Live-Action Moana Makes a Splash — But It’s a Belly Flop
summary: Picture this: you’re sailing across the ocean with Moana, the wind in your hair, adventure ahead. Now replace that with a flat, lifeless screen that one critic compared to a Febreze commercial. That’s the new live-action Moana, and it’s making waves for all the wrong reasons. With a Rotten Tomatoes score of just 33%, it’s one of Disney’s worst-reviewed remakes ever. Only 2000’s 102 Dalmatians (30%), 2016’s Alice Through the Looking Glass (29%), and 2022’s Pinocchio (27%) scored lower. Ouch. Critics didn’t hold back. Clarisse Loughrey of The Independent called Dwayne Johnson’s wig a low point in a film with “all the visual allure of a Febreeze advert.” Others slammed its “AI slop” aesthetic and “creatively empty” soul. The Times’ Kevin Maher even said it provoked “only an exquisite form of agony.” But here’s the kicker: Variety’s Owen Gleiberman praised it because “half the film IS animated.” Wait — isn’t the whole point of a live-action remake to be, well, live-action? That’s like ordering a fresh pizza and getting a frozen one with a sprinkle of cheese on top. It only underlines how unnecessary this whole project feels. Disney has been churning out these remakes since 2010’s Alice in Wonderland, and while some, like 2016’s The Jungle Book, were genuine triumphs, most have been creatively bankrupt cash grabs. Moana 2026 seems destined to join the duds. The irony? The original animated Moana came out just 10 years ago and was a massive hit. Did we really need a do-over so soon? As William Bibbiani of TheWrap put it, “The only time the live-action Moana comes alive is when it’s animated.” Maybe it’s time for Disney to let the past stay in the past and chart a new course. After all, you can’t force the ocean to give you a hit — sometimes, you just have to know when to sail home.
why_it_matters: For a generation growing up with endless remakes, this story shows the danger of valuing profit over originality — and why audiences might start demanding fresh ideas.

background_read: Disney began releasing live-action remakes of its classic animated films in 2010 with Alice in Wonderland, hoping to bring old stories to new audiences using modern visual effects.
Rotten Tomatoes is a well-known review-aggregation website that collects critics’ scores and gives a percentage rating — a low number can hurt a movie’s reputation.
The Independent and TheWrap are major news outlets that publish film reviews; Variety is one of the oldest entertainment trade magazines in the United States.
Some earlier live-action Disney remakes, like 2016’s The Jungle Book, were praised for blending animation and live actors in a fresh way, but many others were criticized for being unnecessary copies.
Article_Structure: LEAD: A vivid contrast between the imagination of a Moana adventure and a lifeless screen, citing a critic’s Febreze-commercial comparison.
KEY EVENT: The live-action Moana earned a Rotten Tomatoes score of just 33%, one of Disney’s worst-reviewed remakes.
├─ COMPARISON: Only three Disney live-action remakes scored lower — 102 Dalmatians (30%), Alice Through the Looking Glass (29%), and Pinocchio (27%).
├─ ONE SIDE: Clarisse Loughrey slammed Dwayne Johnson’s wig; others called the film “AI slop” and “creatively empty”.
└─ UNEXPECTED PRAISE: Variety’s Owen Gleiberman praised it because “half the film IS animated.”
IRONY: The whole point of a live-action remake is to be live-action, but this one relies heavily on animation, undermining its own purpose.
TREND: Disney has been churning out these remakes since 2010, with most being creatively bankrupt cash grabs.
CONCLUSION: The original Moana is only 10 years old; some critics suggest Disney should stop remaking so soon and focus on new stories.

perspectives.description: Fans of Dwayne Johnson or the original Moana might still enjoy seeing a real-world version of the characters, even if the execution was flawed.
Many critics argue the film is a soulless cash grab with no creative purpose, relying too much on lifeless animation and offering nothing new.
From a business standpoint, Disney remakes are safe bets because they profit from nostalgia, but this also creates audience fatigue when quality drops.
The poor reception could push Disney to invest more in original storytelling rather than keep recycling recent hits, or force them to raise the quality of future remakes to rebuild trust.
